textbookText: Class 4: Ciliata i. Body shape is fixed because of the presence of pellicle as external covering. ii. They move with the help of cilia. iii. They are either free living or parasitic. iv. Reproduction by asexually and sexually both.
Activity 8.1 Prepare a power point presentation on the classification kingdom Protista. Present it in the class and discuss.

i. Have you seen the above organism before? What is its shape? ii. Where can it be found? iii. Is it multicellular or unicellular? iv. What might be its locomotory organelles? v. Is it free living or parasitic?

A unicellular, free living and microscopic animalcule called Paramecium is shown in the figure mentioned above. It is found in freshwater rich in decaying organic matter. Its shape is like the sole of slipper, hence called slipper- animalcule. Paramecium moves with the help of minute cytoplasmic hair like projections arising from the general body surface called cilia.

Habit and Habitat Among the several species, Paramecium caudatum is a most common which is found in freshwater like pond, streams, ditches, lakes which are rich in decaying organic matter. They are abundantly found in stagnant water and slow running streams. Paramecium is a free living unicellular microscopic ciliate moving with the help of cilia. It is also called infusorian animalcule as it is found in infusion of decaying animal and vegetable matter.

Activity 8.2 Objective: To identify the various parts of Paramecium Apparatus required: Permanent slide of Paramecium, microscope Procedure: i. Fix a permanent slide of Paramecium under a microscope. ii. Observe the slide. iii. Note down the structures seen on the chart paper. (Take the help of your teacher, if necessary). iv. Search on the internet more about Paramecium. v. Draw a labelled diagram and discuss. Conclusion

A. External structure (Morphology) a. Shape and size Paramecium caudatum has slipper shaped or spindle shaped cell body so it is commonly called the ‘Slipper Animalcule’. Its body is asymmetrical due to the presence of obliquely situated oral groove. Body is elongated and blunt at the anterior end, wider just below the middle region and somewhat pointed at the posterior end. Its ventral side is flat and marks the oral surface and dorsal side is called the aboral surface. It is a microscopic organism and visible to the naked eye as a whitish or greyish spot. Among the several species, Paramecium caudatum is the largest measuring about 170µ-290 µ in length.

Figure 8.1.6 Paramecium caudatum b. Pellicle: Body of Paramecium is externally covered by a thin, double layered, elastic and gelatinous protective membrane called pellicle. Elastic nature of pellicle facilitates the organism to squeeze or pass through narrow places. Under high power microscope, the pellicle consists of regular series of hexagonal shaped depressions and from the centre of each hexagonal shape emerges out a cilium. The anterior and posterior margin of the hexagonal depressions have opening for the discharge of trichocyst.

c. Cilia: The whole body of Paramecium is covered by numerous tiny hair like projections called cilia. Cilia are uniform sized and arranged in longitudinal rows except at the posterior end, where they are the long tuft, forming caudal tuft. Each cilium arises from a spherical basal granule or kinetosome lying just below the pellicle in ectoplasm. Cilia are use by the organism for locomotion, food capturing and also as sensory receptors which respond to external stimuli. Caudal tuft helps to change the direction while swimming.

B. Internal structure a. Cytoplasm Cytoplasm of Paramecium is clearly differentiated into two regions. i. Ectoplasm: It is a thin, peripheral, clear and dense region of cytoplasm which includes trichocyst, basal bodies and fibrils. ii. Endoplasm: It is the large central, granular and semifluid region which contains cell components such as nucleus, contractile vacuole, food vacuoles, mitochondria, golgibodies, ribosomes etc.
